sources.title: Kazuo Ishiguro (Q272855) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-23): English label 'Kazuo Ishiguro', description 'British novelist (born 1954)', born 1954-11-08, no date of death, place of birth Nagasaki, citizenship listed as United Kingdom and Japan, Korean label '가즈오 이시구로', P18 images including a 2017 Stockholm photograph. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

'Ishiguro Wins Nobel Prize in Literature', Shelf Awareness, 5 October 2017, read in full: the Swedish Academy's citation ('in novels of great emotional force, has uncovered the abyss beneath our illusory sense of connection with the world'), permanent secretary Sara Danius's remarks (a 'writer of great integrity' who 'doesn't look to the side' and has 'developed an aesthetic universe all his own', blending Austen, Kafka and Proust with restraint), the honours listed (Whitbread 1986, Booker 1989, OBE 1995, Chevalier de l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres 1998), the eight works named, the Guardian's note that bookmakers favoured others, and Salman Rushdie's congratulation noting that Ishiguro also plays guitar and writes songs. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (trade press reporting the award body's citation; the nobelprize.org pages returned an access error and were not opened). The praise is the Academy's and a friend's, so it is retrospective and admiring.

Harry Ransom Center (University of Texas at Austin) press release on its 2015 acquisition of the Kazuo Ishiguro archive, read in full: Booker Prize for The Remains of the Day (1989) and Whitbread Book of the Year for An Artist of the Floating World (1986), the novels from A Pale View of Hills (1982) to The Buried Giant (2015), the archive's thousands of preparatory notes and drafts for each novel by a writer who 'works slowly', a document called 'HOW I WRITE', yellow sticky-note annotations, two early unpublished novels, songwriting, a pulp Western, and the screenplays (The Saddest Music in the World, The White Countess, and two Channel 4 originals); the director's remark on how fully the archive shows memory's ties to his art. Institutional archive record; independent of the author but descriptive and admiring, and the archive's contents themselves were not examined.

Encyclopedia.com entry on 'The Remains of the Day' (Gale 'Novels for Students' reference material), read to the page's cut-off: author biography (born in Nagasaki, to England as a child, honours degree in philosophy and literature 1978, University of East Anglia creative-writing master's 1980, social work before writing full time, OBE 1995), the novel's 1988 publication and 1989 Booker Prize, the 1993 Merchant Ivory film, and a spread of named critical reactions from Graver, Rushdie, Rubin, Gurewich, Lee, Hassan, Kakutani, Coates and Strawson (praise) to Geoff Dyer (narrative irony 'trite', voice 'coaxed') and Gabriele Annan (didactic, read as anti-Japanese). The family details on the page were not used. Independent reference compilation including dissent; the final fifth of the page was not read.

'Never Let Me Go: A Profile of Kazuo Ishiguro', Poets & Writers (2005), read in full: the profile writer's observations that he began Never Let Me Go as a 1950s lounge-singer story, switched to a cloning premise after a dinner conversation and a year later abandoned the original setting, that the book is his most radical stylistic departure with a world the reader must infer, Ishiguro's own words ('I don't think in terms of genre at all'; he must be careful not to repeat his devices), critic James Wood's 'reliably unreliable' narrators, the 'voluptuously deceptive storyteller' description, starred pre-publication reviews, and his early songwriting. Independent interview-based press profile mixing the writer's observations and the subject's own words; the two are separated in the rows.

John O'Neill, 'Neil Gaiman and Ursula K. Le Guin on Kazuo Ishiguro's The Buried Giant', Black Gate, 7 March 2015, read in full: Le Guin's blog objection to what she read as Ishiguro's disdain for fantasy while using its 'surface elements' (quoting his remark in a New York Times interview asking whether readers would be 'prejudiced against the surface elements' and say 'this is fantasy'), her description of reading the book as painful, and Neil Gaiman's largely positive New York Times review that admits an 'inability to fall in love with it'. Counter-voice source about a single book; the page reproduces Le Guin and Gaiman second-hand, contains no reply from Ishiguro, and a commenter's summary of Le Guin is not used.

Penguin Random House page for the Everyman's Library edition of 'Never Let Me Go', including an author interview, read in full: Ishiguro's own account of writing pieces about students over about fifteen years, repeatedly setting the idea aside to write other novels, and of a radio discussion of biotechnology that made the framework fall into place; his choice of a 1970s-80s English setting rather than a future one, of a less guarded narrator, and his wish for 'unfilmable' novels; plus publisher copy and review blurbs. Mostly SELF material (an author interview on a publisher's page, promotional in purpose) and counted as the self perspective only; not the sole support for any row.

Wikimedia Commons file page 'Kazuo Ishiguro in Stockholm 2017 02.jpg' (wikitext and API record) -- checked for the portrait's licence: own work by Frankie Fouganthin, taken 6 December 2017 at the Swedish Academy's press conference in Stockholm, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 by the photographer; original 1219 x 1500 pixels. Not used for any scoring.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_ishiguro_shelf, src_ishiguro_pw, src_ishiguro_blackgate, src_ishiguro_remains | 1980s-2015 | award citation + profile + critics] The Swedish Academy credits novels of 'great emotional force' and an 'aesthetic universe all his own'; the Poets & Writers profile calls Never Let Me Go his most radical stylistic departure, and critics describe his unreliable narrators as taken to an artistic zenith. The counter-voices are real (Dyer finds the irony trite, Le Guin and Gaiman are cool on The Buried Giant), and much of the praise is retrospective, so the score is held in the low 70s. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a highest-risk row (retrospective award praise) and left unchanged because the profile and the named critics add contemporaneous, independent assessment and the confidence is already below 0.65.

experimentation.rationale: [src_ishiguro_shelf, src_ishiguro_pw, src_ishiguro_blackgate, src_ishiguro_hrc | 1982-2015 | citation + profile + critics + archive] The eight works named by the Academy move from postwar Japan to an English butler, orphans, a clone-themed school story and a fantasy-tinged quest; the profile quotes him on varying his devices and reports a radical stylistic shift in Never Let Me Go; screenplays and songwriting are in the archive. The Buried Giant drew a public genre dispute, so the formal risk-taking is real, but how deliberate each shift was rests largely on his own remarks.

persistence.rationale: [src_ishiguro_hrc, src_ishiguro_pw, src_ishiguro_penguin | 1990-2005 | archive + profile + author interview] The archive holds thousands of preparatory notes and drafts for each novel by a writer described as working slowly; the profile reports that Never Let Me Go went through an abandoned first setting, and Ishiguro says (self) he returned to the students idea over about fifteen years. The duration is mostly his own account; the independent sources show slow, repeated reworking, not the length of the span.

detail_orientation.rationale: [src_ishiguro_hrc, src_ishiguro_pw | 2015 archive, 2005 profile | archive + profile] The archive's volume of notes and annotated drafts and the profile's picture of a tightly controlled technique are consistent with exacting attention to craft detail, but no source read documents specific revisions or standards. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a highest-risk row (indirect inference from archive volume) and lowered from 66 / 0.52 to 60 / 0.46 because the archive shows how much he kept, not how exacting each revision was, and the 'controlled' praise elsewhere is partly publisher blurb.

adaptability.rationale: [src_ishiguro_pw, src_ishiguro_penguin | 1990s-2005 | profile + author interview] The profile reports that he dropped a lounge-singer story after a dinner conversation and, a year later, abandoned the original setting for a cloning premise; in his own account he set the students idea aside repeatedly and picked it up again when a new framework appeared. This shows changing course on a project in response to a new idea, not a general trait; one project only.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_ishiguro_hrc, src_ishiguro_shelf, src_ishiguro_pw | 1980s-2000s | archive + press + profile] Beyond novels and short stories, the archive documents screenplays (The Saddest Music in the World, The White Countess, two Channel 4 originals), songwriting and a pulp Western; Rushdie's congratulation notes guitar and songs, and the profile says he wrote and recorded demos. Range is documented but secondary to the novels; the quality and reach of the non-novel work is not assessed.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: wbgetentities (2026-10-23) for Q272855 returned en label 'Kazuo Ishiguro', description 'British novelist (born 1954)', born 1954-11-08, no death date, place of birth Nagasaki, ko label '가즈오 이시구로'; the lead's hint is correct. Wikidata lists citizenship as United Kingdom and Japan; nationalityCodes uses GB only, following the Academy's and the sources' description of him as a British/English novelist, so the Japan entry is flagged for lead judgement. SLUG/QID CHECK: grep found no existing candidate or person for slug kazuo-ishiguro or QID Q272855. REGION: western_europe, era contemporary, LIVING. ZERO POLITICS passes (novelist; no political content scored). LIVING-SUBJECT RULE: only public professional behaviour is scored; family, health and private life are not used (the biography page's family lines and any personal-history framing were ignored). VOCABULARY: occupation writer, field literature, impact domains literary and cultural, tags nobel_laureate and craft_focused, archetype creative_creator (all used elsewhere). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Shelf Awareness 'Ishiguro Wins Nobel Prize in Literature' (https://shelf-awareness.com/theshelf/2017-10-05/ishiguro_wins_nobel_prize_in_literature.html), a trade-press report of the Swedish Academy citation, because nobelprize.org returned 403 (substitute noted); the Encyclopedia.com entry also gives the Booker/OBE context. EVIDENCE READ: 6 substantive sources (Shelf Awareness; Harry Ransom Center press release; Encyclopedia.com 'Remains of the Day' entry; Poets & Writers 2005 profile; Black Gate on the Le Guin/Gaiman response to The Buried Giant; the Penguin Random House author interview) plus Wikidata and a Commons file page as orientation. PERSPECTIVES: award body (via press), an independent archive, a reference compilation with named dissenters (Dyer, Annan), an independent press profile quoting critic James Wood, counter-voices (Le Guin, Gaiman's reservation, Dyer), and the subject himself (publisher interview plus quotations in the profile, counted as the self perspective). Non-self behavioural sources: the HRC archive description and the Poets & Writers profile. NOT OPENED or failed: nobelprize.org facts and press release (403), Booker Prizes site (403), enotes critical overview (403), CNBC (403), Boing Boing and writingroutines.com accounts of the four-week 1987 drafting of The Remains of the Day (403 and a certificate error), so that well-known story is NOT used; the Paris Review interview, the Nobel lecture, The Guardian and New Yorker pieces, and Ishiguro's reply to Le Guin (reported only in search summaries) were not read. EXCLUSIONS: wife, daughter, birth family and emigration, health, childhood, the Booker judges' dispute (single secondary report), music quality and fame as trait evidence, film adaptations (side outcome), prize prestige as a trait. THIN ROWS: six rows only; collaboration, conflict_tolerance, independent_thinking and discipline were considered and left unscored (single quoted remark, retrospective praise only, or no behavioural source read). SOURCE-COUNT NOTE: six substantive sources is the floor of the cost-cap range; the Penguin interview is self-promotional and the HRC release is descriptive, so the independent behavioural base is narrow, which is why the highest score is 72 and the highest confidence 0.60. PORTRAIT: Commons page checked (own work, Frankie Fouganthin, 6 December 2017, CC BY-SA 4.0 via the {{self}} template, no restrictions field, original 1219x1500, categories Kazuo Ishiguro and Nobel Prize in Literature 2017); preferred over the 360x450 CC BY 2.5 P18 file (Mariusz Kubik, 2005) for size; a Swedish Academy or Nobel Foundation image was not sought (the Nobel site is blocked for automated reading and its terms were not read); file downscaled to 975x1200 (JPEG q88) and inspected: single subject, face clear, tightly cropped with a headset microphone visible. SELF-CALIBRATION PASS: reviewed creative_originality (retrospective praise) and detail_orientation (indirect inference) and persistence (mostly self-account); lowered detail_orientation only (66/0.52 to 60/0.46); creative_originality and persistence left unchanged with reasons in their rationales. No eligibility or match output was used in scoring.
